prompt: What does a confirmed address prove?

choices.text: That the person gave their real name
choices.why: The link says nothing about the name typed beside the address.

choices.text: The person who signed up has access to that inbox
choices.why: Right: that is all it proves, and it is what the flow is for.

choices.text: That every later e-mail will be delivered to that inbox
choices.why: Delivery can still fail later; confirmation is about one moment.

choices.text: That the address belongs to a member of the theatre
choices.why: Confirming makes the account a member; it does not check that it already was one.

prompt: Why is the token in a confirmation link treated as a secret?

choices.text: It contains the account's password in a coded form
choices.why: It is random; it carries no password, coded or not.

choices.text: Mail servers refuse to deliver links they can read
choices.why: Mail servers deliver links all the time; the risk is who holds it.

choices.text: Whoever holds it confirms the account, no password needed
choices.why: Right: so it must be unguessable and live in the e-mail only.

choices.text: It shows which other accounts exist at the theatre
choices.why: One token stands for one account and says nothing about others.

prompt: Asking for a new link answers the same sentence whether or not the address has an account. Why is that right?

choices.text: A different answer would reveal who has an account
choices.why: Right: the form would become a way to ask about a particular person.

choices.text: It is cheaper to write one message than two
choices.why: Cost is not the reason; the second message would leak information.

choices.text: R7 forbids error messages, so nothing can say the account is missing
choices.why: R7 asks for a sentence instead of an error page, and allows saying what is wrong.

choices.text: The application cannot tell whether an account exists
choices.why: It can: it checks before deciding whether to send.

prompt: Match each case to its expected result.
hint: One expected result is not written anywhere.

pairs.left: Open the old link after asking for a new one
Open a link that already confirmed the account
Ask for a link for an address with no account
pairs.right: The same answer, and no e-mail

right_distractors: An error page saying the account is missing

prompt: On staging, every case passes in the catcher, but a customer's link in production opens the test server. Which case should have caught it?

choices.text: Opening the link within 24 hours
choices.why: That passed: on staging the link opens staging, which is where it was opened.

choices.text: Reading the e-mail: a link to the right site
choices.why: Right: the link is built from settings, and settings differ per environment.

choices.text: Asking for a new link and opening the old one
choices.why: That checks the life of a token, not where the link points.

choices.text: Changing one character of the token
choices.why: That checks the token is refused; the host is the same.

prompt: Why does a test build catch its e-mail instead of sending it?
hint: Think of a run with copied data.

choices.text: Sending e-mail is too slow for a test run
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; who receives it is.

choices.text: Mail servers reject messages sent from a laptop
choices.why: Some do, and that is not why boxoffice catches its mail.

choices.text: So no test reaches a real person
choices.why: Right, and so the tester can read every message.

choices.text: Because the requirements forbid e-mail outside production
choices.why: No requirement says so; R3 only says an e-mail is sent.

prompt: Every address in this course ends in example.___, a domain reserved for examples and documentation.
Caio's link confirmed his account and, opened again, says "Your account is confirmed." again. What do you do?
hint: What does R3 say about it?

choices.text: Report a defect: links must be single use
choices.why: R3 never says so, so there is no expected result to fail.

choices.text: Ask the theatre, with the observation attached
choices.why: Right: R3 is silent, so it is a question for the client.

choices.text: Nothing: anything the requirements do not mention is acceptable
choices.why: Silence is a gap to raise, not a permission.

choices.text: Restart boxoffice and repeat it until the second open fails
choices.why: Repeating the same steps gives the same result; the question is what is expected.

prompt: Order the steps that show defect 10.
hint: The old link must exist before the new one.
items: Sign up a new account, Dora Reis
Ask for a new link at /resend
Find Dora's first link in the outbox, second in the list
Open that first link and read the answer
trap: Opening the first link before asking again confirms the account and leaves nothing to test.

prompt: Why does defect 10 matter more than it looks?
hint: Why do people ask for a second link?

choices.text: Each extra link costs the theatre an e-mail it pays for
choices.why: The outbox shows the messages are sent either way; the risk is the live link.

choices.text: Customers cannot confirm their account until it is fixed
choices.why: Both links confirm; nobody is locked out.

choices.text: The first link is in an inbox the person no longer watches
choices.why: Right: an old address, a shared inbox, a typo; and it keeps working after the person thought it was shut.

choices.text: The new link stops working while the old one is still live
choices.why: The capture never tried the new link after the old one; nothing shows that.

prompt: Started a day later, Dora's old link was refused. Started at the original time, it was refused too. What does the second run show?
hint: What else did the restart do?

choices.text: That links expire much sooner than 24 hours
choices.why: No time passed in the second run; expiry cannot explain it.

choices.text: That BOXOFFICE_NOW was ignored both times
choices.why: boxoffice read it at start-up; the clock was not the problem.

choices.text: That expiry works, because both answers agree
choices.why: Agreement is the problem: the test gives the same answer either way.

choices.text: The restart erased the link, so the first run tested nothing
choices.why: Right: a test that cannot fail measures nothing; expiry is still untested.

prompt: What is the rule for anything sent to a public Mailinator inbox?

choices.text: Use it only for accounts with a strong password
choices.why: A reset link sent there would take the account whatever its password.

choices.text: Test data only, never real data
choices.why: Right: anybody who types the same name reads the same messages.

choices.text: Delete each message after reading it, so nobody else sees it
choices.why: Somebody may read it first; the inbox is public from the moment it arrives.

choices.text: Use a long, unusual name and real data is then safe
choices.why: A hard name is still a public inbox; it hides nothing from somebody who has it.

prompt: Match each tool to what it is.
hint: One of them is the outbox's idea again.

pairs.right: A catcher you run that pretends to be a mail server
Public, disposable inboxes anybody can read
A package a test uses to read a real Gmail inbox

prompt: What can a catcher such as Mailpit not tell you?

choices.text: Which address the application wrote in the To line
choices.why: It keeps the whole message, recipient included.

choices.text: Whether the confirmation link carries a token
choices.why: The body is right there to read.

choices.text: Whether a real mail server would deliver it at all
choices.why: Right: spam filters and real delivery happen after the point it stops.

choices.text: How many messages the application sent during a run
choices.why: It keeps every one, so counting them is easy.

prompt: A test account ana.tests@gmail.com must receive each case's mail separately. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: Gmail ignores part of the address.

choices.text: Create a separate Gmail account for each case
choices.why: It works, and it multiplies credentials to guard; one inbox suffices.

choices.text: Sign up as ana.tests+case4@gmail.com
choices.why: Right: it lands in the same inbox and the case is in the address.

choices.text: Use Mailinator for the cases and Gmail for the rest
choices.why: Moving cases to a public inbox trades separation for exposure.

choices.text: Delete every message before the next case starts
choices.why: A late message from the last case then lands in the next one unnoticed.

prompt: A product's password-reset e-mail works like boxoffice's confirmation: asking again leaves the old link alive. Which case finds it?

choices.text: Ask twice, then open the first link that was sent
choices.why: Right: case 4 transfers to any link that can be asked for again.

choices.text: Open the newest link within its time limit
choices.why: That passes whether or not the old one died.

choices.text: Change a character of the token in the newest link
choices.why: That checks forged tokens are refused, not old ones.

choices.text: Ask for a reset for an address with no account
choices.why: That checks what the form reveals, not the life of a link.

prompt: By R3, for how many hours is a confirmation link valid if nobody asks for another?
hint: It is in the e-mail too.

prompt: Until a clock can move while boxoffice runs, case 3, expiry, is reported as not ___.
A team tests sign-up on staging, which sends real e-mail, with copies of real customers' names. Which inbox fits?

choices.text: Mailinator, with a fresh name for each case
choices.why: Real names in a public inbox are exactly what its rule forbids.

choices.text: The customers' own addresses, since the data is theirs
choices.why: Then real people receive test mail, which a catcher exists to prevent.

choices.text: A catcher such as Mailpit, pointed at by staging
choices.why: Right: nothing leaves the team's machines, and the data stays there too.

choices.text: Any public inbox, as long as the messages are deleted the same day
choices.why: Deletion comes after somebody may already have read them.
